title: Picky eating
byline: Being wary of new food is a normal toddler stage. Your child’s growth, not today’s plate, tells you when to ask for help.
image_alt: Soft bread, yogurt, and two broccoli florets

findings.lead: Wariness of new foods peaks after the first birthday.
findings.text: A child who ate everything as a baby and gets fussier as a toddler is on a very common path. Nobody has failed.

findings.lead: Keep the routine, drop the negotiating.
findings.text: One family meal, a familiar food on the plate, and no separate dinner on request.

findings.lead: Ask for help when growth is the worry, not table manners.
findings.text: Dropping off a growth curve, fear around eating that looks like pain, or months of eating only a handful of foods is a question for a doctor.

sections.heading: What’s normal
paragraphs: Wariness of new food rises in the second year and then slowly eases. It probably helped keep children safe once they could wander off towards unknown plants. It can feel personal, but it’s mostly a developmental stage. Children also have days of eating almost nothing and days of eating loads, often in step with growth spurts rather than your menu.

A few reliable foods, sometimes called safe foods, are a real asset. Build the plate around one of them, plus some of the family meal. Don’t give up on a food for good just because it was refused twice.

sections.heading: What helps
paragraphs: Keep meals predictable. Let your child see the food without being asked to do anything with it. Eat the same food yourself. Offer refused foods cut a different way or next to a dip they like, still without comment. Fifteen quiet offers beat one big tasting showdown.

After the first birthday, milk shouldn’t take the place of meals. A toddler who drinks milk all afternoon will arrive at dinner full. Give water between meals and milk with a meal or snack, in a moderate amount over the day.

sections.heading: When it’s more than fussiness
paragraphs: Talk to your health visitor or paediatrician if weight or length gain is stalling, if eating seems to hurt, if your child coughs or vomits with certain textures, or if the list of accepted foods has shrunk to a few specific brands and keeps shrinking. More pressure won’t fix these patterns.
A child who is growing, playing, and driving you mad at dinner is usually completely ordinary. Your job is to stay calm, predictable, and available.

title: When your child is ill
byline: Familiar food, enough fluids, and the usual milk feeds. A sick day is the wrong day to decide on an allergy or try a new food.
image_alt: Thin oat porridge and a small dish of yogurt

findings.lead: Fluids and milk come before a perfect menu.
findings.text: Small, familiar meals are enough. Don’t make a young child go without food.

findings.lead: Don’t introduce a new allergen while your child is ill.
findings.text: You can’t tell what a rash or vomiting means on that day.

findings.lead: Know the signs that need a doctor the same day.
findings.text: Few wet nappies, a sunken soft spot (fontanelle), blood in the stool, unusual sleepiness, or laboured breathing are not things to watch and wait on at home.

sections.heading: Feeding a poorly child
paragraphs: Fever and a sore mouth both dampen appetite. Keep up breast milk or formula. Offer smaller amounts of foods your child already likes: yogurt, fruit, plain porridge, or unsalted broth is enough. Pushing a balanced plate on a child who feels sick can put them off food.

If your child is vomiting or has diarrhoea and milk alone isn’t keeping up, oral rehydration solution is the right tool. Your health visitor can talk you through it. Sugary juice is a poor substitute and can make diarrhoea worse.

sections.heading: Save new foods for a healthy week
paragraphs: Illness changes skin and stools. A new food on the same day can create a false allergy story, and a food the family then avoids for years. Wait until your child is well, then pick up the introduction plan again.
Teething and illness often get blamed for each other. More than a slight temperature, or a child who is clearly unwell, can’t be put down to a tooth. Get them checked.

sections.heading: When to call a doctor
paragraphs: Call the same day if your child is under three months old and has a fever, is unusually floppy or hard to wake, is struggling to breathe, has blood in their vomit or stool, or isn’t passing urine. In these situations, food advice doesn’t matter.
After antibiotics, there’s no need for a special ‘cleanse’. Ordinary food is fine, including yogurt if they like it. Probiotics are optional, not a necessary part of recovery.

title: Teething
byline: Cold food and something firm to chew are enough. Skip amber necklaces and benzocaine gels.
image_alt: A chilled cucumber baton and cold strawberry purée

findings.text: A chilled cucumber stick, a cold spoon, or a half-frozen fruit purée can help, if that texture is already safe for your baby.

findings.lead: Skip benzocaine and lidocaine teething gels.
findings.text: Regulators warn against them for babies because they can affect how blood carries oxygen and because they numb the gag reflex.

findings.lead: Amber necklaces are a strangling and choking hazard.
findings.text: There’s no good evidence that they ease pain, and there are reports of harm.

sections.heading: What helps at the table
paragraphs: Teething can make gums sore and meals smaller for a few days. Keep offering the usual foods. Add something cold the baby can already manage: yogurt from the fridge, a peeled cucumber stick if they are chewing soft strips, or a fruit purée frozen until it is spoonable rather than rock hard. A hard lump of ice is its own choking and tooth injury.
Extra drool plus acidic fruit often reddens the chin. A plain barrier ointment and gentle washing do more than an allergy label. Wipe, do not scrub.

sections.heading: Gels and tablets
paragraphs: The US Food and Drug Administration advises against benzocaine teething products in children under two, because of methemoglobinaemia, and against viscous lidocaine for the same job. Numbing the mouth also makes choking more likely. In Europe, products aimed at infant teething have been restricted for the same reasons.

A clean finger rubbed on the gum is dull and effective. A dose of paracetamol or ibuprofen, in the infant formulation and at the dose your clinician has already approved, is the medicine conversation to have. It is not a food decision, and it is not for every grizzle.

sections.heading: Necklaces and other objects
paragraphs: Amber bead necklaces are marketed as a natural analgesic. The proposed mechanism is not credible at the dose a bead could release onto skin, and the object sits on the airway. The FDA has warned about choking and strangulation. Take them off for sleep and, better, do not use them.
Teething biscuits that are rock hard, or that are mostly sugar, fail both the choking test and the nutrition test. A piece of bread crust the baby already manages is a simpler chew.

title: Vitamins and minerals
byline: Vitamin D is a supplement decision from the first days. Iron is a food decision from six months. Everything else follows from the diet.
image_alt: Cooked chicken liver, apple, egg, and red lentils

findings.lead: Breastfed babies need a vitamin D supplement.
findings.text: Food won’t cover it. In Hungary, the usual preventive dose is prescribed by the paediatrician or health visitor, often 400 IU a day.

findings.lead: After six months, iron comes from food, not a routine tonic.
findings.text: The sources are meat, legumes, and fortified cereal. Iron supplements are for a diagnosed deficiency or a specific risk, not for everyone.

findings.lead: A vegan diet for a baby needs a plan, not hope.
findings.text: Vitamin B12, iodine, iron, zinc, calcium, and DHA won’t turn up by accident in a plant-only diet.

findings.lead: Liver is a dose of vitamin A.
findings.text: One small portion a week is plenty. Don’t add a vitamin A supplement on top.

sections.heading: Vitamin D
paragraphs: Infants in Central Europe do not make enough vitamin D from sun for most of the year, and breast milk contains little. The NHS recommends 8.5 to 10 micrograms (340 to 400 IU) a day for breastfed babies from birth to one year. Hungarian paediatric practice commonly prescribes a daily vitamin D drop in that neighbourhood, sometimes up to a higher prevention dose. Use the product and the dose you were given. Do not stack a second product ‘to be safe’.

Infant formula already contains vitamin D. A baby drinking around 500 ml or more a day may not need an extra drop; this is a question for the prescriber, because the right answer depends on the formula and the volume.

sections.heading: Iron, zinc, and iodine
paragraphs: The dietary iron need in the second six months is high relative to body size, about 11 mg a day in US reference values, and it is met by food frequency rather than by one heroic portion. Serve an iron food most days. Zinc travels with meat and with beans. Plants alone are a thinner zinc source.

Iodine matters for the thyroid and for development. Dairy, eggs, and fish carry it. Iodised salt is the population tool and is the wrong tool under one year, because salt itself is restricted. A breastfeeding mother’s iodine intake matters; that is her supplement conversation, not a reason to salt the baby.

sections.heading: Vegetarian and vegan plates
paragraphs: A lacto-ovo vegetarian infant diet can work if eggs and dairy are actually eaten and iron is planned. A vegan diet can be constructed and is easy to get wrong. ESPGHAN asks that vegan infants receive medical and dietetic supervision and a reliable vitamin B12 source. Iodine, DHA from an algal oil, iron, zinc, and calcium need named foods, not a hope that variety will cover them.
Plant drinks are not infant formula. Rice drinks are unsuitable under five. Other plant drinks are not a main drink in the first year unless a clinician has chosen a specific product.

sections.heading: Vitamin A and the liver rule
paragraphs: Liver is rich in iron and so rich in preformed vitamin A that a large or frequent portion can overshoot. A small serving, about 15 grams of cooked liver in the child’s share, at most once a week, is the cautious reading of that fact. Skip liver entirely in a week when a vitamin A containing supplement is being used.
Ordinary vegetables supply carotenoids, which the body converts in a regulated way. There is no matching limit on carrots. Orange skin from carrots is harmless and fades.

title: A pocket guide
byline: The decisions that matter, on one page, with links to the longer explanations.
image_alt: Minced chicken with soft carrot and pear

findings.lead: Start around six months, with iron and the main allergens.
findings.text: Keep up milk feeds. Move textures on. Eat together. Calmly offer refused foods again.

findings.lead: Leave out honey, added salt, added sugar, and whole nuts.
findings.text: Leave out juice, rice drinks, ham, stock cubes, and hard round foods.

findings.lead: Ask a clinician before peanut if eczema is severe or egg allergy is already known.
findings.text: Get help the same day if breathing, colour, or responsiveness changes after a food.

sections.heading: Do
paragraphs: Wait until your baby is developing the skills to eat, and start by about six months, but not before four. Offer meat, lentils, beans, egg, or fortified cereal early. Offer peanut, egg, milk, wheat, sesame, fish, and soy in safe textures, and once they’re tolerated, keep them in the weekly routine. Sit your baby upright. Add a little oil. Use herbs. Freeze unsalted leftovers.
If you’d like the reasoning behind the list, read the pages on timing, allergens, and how mealtimes work.

sections.heading: Do not
paragraphs: Do not add salt or sugar. Do not give honey before one year. Do not give whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, or thick nut butter. Do not give rice drinks to a child under five. Do not use cow’s milk as the main drink before one. Do not serve liver more than once a week. Do not keep a raw herb paste for a week or store garlic in oil. Do not feed from a screen or bargain with dessert.

Party cakes, chocolate bars, and crunchy granola are occasional foods for older toddlers, and many familiar versions have the wrong texture or the wrong sweetener for a baby. The recipe pages explain what was changed and why.

sections.heading: Ask someone
paragraphs: Before the first taste of peanut, if your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy. If your baby isn’t growing well. If you’re feeding a vegan diet. If a food caused hives all over, swelling, breathing difficulty, or floppiness: that last group needs emergency care, not an appointment next week.
This site is an evidence-checked companion inspired by a Hungarian weaning book. It isn’t that book, and it isn’t personal medical advice about your child.
